blocks.alt: Original handwritten student working for analysis

children.prompt: What did Yetta do wrong while adding the fractions?

answer.short: She added the numerators and the denominators. The denominators must be made the same before adding the numerators.
answer.worked:
She added the numerators and the denominators separately. First rewrite the fractions with a common denominator, then add the numerators.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{4}&=\frac{8}{20}+\frac{15}{20}\\&=\frac{23}{20}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Is Yetta’s answer bigger or smaller than the correct answer? How can you tell?

answer.short: Smaller. $\frac{5}{9}<\frac{3}{4}$, but adding the positive fraction $\frac{2}{5}$ to $\frac{3}{4}$ gives a result greater than $\frac{3}{4}$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{5}{9}&=\frac{20}{36}\\\frac{3}{4}&=\frac{27}{36}\end{align*}$$
So $\frac{5}{9}<\frac{3}{4}$. The correct sum is greater than $\frac{3}{4}$ because $\frac{2}{5}$ is positive. Yetta’s answer is smaller.

inlines.text: He reads the rest over the weekend.
How much of the book did he read over the weekend?

answer.worked:
Read before the weekend:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{5}{36}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{6}&=\frac{5}{36}+\frac{4}{36}+\frac{6}{36}\\&=\frac{15}{36}=\frac{5}{12}\end{align*}$$
Read over the weekend:
$$\begin{align*}1-\frac{5}{12}&=\frac{12}{12}-\frac{5}{12}\\&=\frac{7}{12}\end{align*}$$
He read $\frac{7}{12}$ of the book over the weekend.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise efficient grouping by common denominator and explain the method.

answer.short: $2\frac{3}{4}$. Group and add fractions with the same denominator.
answer.worked:
Group fractions with the same denominator to avoid finding a common denominator for all six fractions.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{3}{7}+\frac{4}{13}+\frac{5}{8}+\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{7}+\frac{1}{8}
&=\left(\frac{3}{7}+\frac{4}{7}\right)+\left(\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}\right)+\left(\frac{5}{8}+\frac{1}{8}\right)\\
&=\frac{7}{7}+\frac{13}{13}+\frac{6}{8}\\
&=1+1+\frac{3}{4}\\
&=2\frac{3}{4}.
\end{align*}$$

The missing fraction is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}&=\frac{5}{15}-\frac{3}{15}\\&=\frac{2}{15}.\end{align*}$$

The missing fraction is

The missing denominator is $7$.

The missing fraction is

The missing denominator is $4$.

spec.description: Central square containing 5; three blank squares above, three below, two left and two right. Four curved directed paths connect the outer squares. White interiors, black outlines and operation labels; ten handwriting boxes.
spec.mathematics: Upper arm subtracts 1/2 three times. Lower arm subtracts 1 1/3 three times. Left arm subtracts 2 1/6 twice. Right arm subtracts 13/8 then 11/8. Outer paths add 17/6 from left to top, subtract 1 1/2 from top to right, subtract 1 from right to bottom, and subtract 1/3 from bottom to left.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the central 5 and all supplied operation labels are visible. All ten response squares remain empty.

answer.short: Above the centre, nearest to farthest: $4\frac12,\ 4,\ 3\frac12$. Below: $3\frac23,\ 2\frac13,\ 1$. Left: $2\frac56,\ \frac23$. Right: $3\frac38,\ 2$.
answer.worked:
Above the centre:
$$\begin{align*}5-\frac12&=\frac{10}{2}-\frac12=4\frac12\\4\frac12-\frac12&=4\\4-\frac12&=\frac82-\frac12=3\frac12\end{align*}$$
Below the centre:
$$\begin{align*}5-1\frac13&=\frac{15}{3}-\frac43=\frac{11}{3}=3\frac23\\3\frac23-1\frac13&=\frac{11}{3}-\frac43=\frac73=2\frac13\\2\frac13-1\frac13&=\frac73-\frac43=1\end{align*}$$
Left of the centre:
$$\begin{align*}5-2\frac16&=\frac{30}{6}-\frac{13}{6}=\frac{17}{6}=2\frac56\\2\frac56-2\frac16&=\frac{17}{6}-\frac{13}{6}=\frac46=\frac23\end{align*}$$
Right of the centre:
$$\begin{align*}5-\frac{13}{8}&=\frac{40}{8}-\frac{13}{8}=\frac{27}{8}=3\frac38\\3\frac38-\frac{11}{8}&=\frac{27}{8}-\frac{11}{8}=\frac{16}{8}=2\end{align*}$$
The outer paths agree:
$$\begin{align*}\frac23+\frac{17}{6}&=\frac46+\frac{17}{6}=\frac{21}{6}=3\frac12\\3\frac12-1\frac12&=\frac72-\frac32=2\\2-1&=1\\1-\frac13&=\frac33-\frac13=\frac23\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let the missing length be $x$ cm. The perimeters are equal.
$$\begin{align*}
P_A&=2\left(2\frac{3}{4}+4\frac{1}{6}\right)\text{ cm}\\
P_A&=13\frac{5}{6}\text{ cm}\\
P_B&=\left(2x+2\left(6\frac{2}{3}\right)\right)\text{ cm}\\
P_B&=\left(2x+13\frac{1}{3}\right)\text{ cm}\\
2x&=13\frac{5}{6}-13\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\\
x&=\frac{1}{4}
\end{align*}$$
The missing length is $\frac{1}{4}\text{ cm}$.

inlines.text: Using a calculator, or mentally, complete the table.
Smaller, equal, or larger compared to original?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}12\times0.5&=6\end{align*}$$
Since $0.5<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}7\times1&=7\end{align*}$$
Multiplying by $1$ leaves the original number unchanged.

$$\begin{align*}15\times1.5&=22.5\end{align*}$$
Since $1.5>1$, the product is larger than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}20\times0.2&=4\end{align*}$$
Since $0.2<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}10\times2.5&=25\end{align*}$$
Since $2.5>1$, the product is larger than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}5\times0.2&=1\end{align*}$$
Since $0.2<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}40\times0.9&=36\end{align*}$$
Since $0.9<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}6\times1.1&=6.6\end{align*}$$
Since $1.1>1$, the product is larger than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}12\times\frac{1}{3}&=4\end{align*}$$
Since $\frac{1}{3}<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}20\times\frac{3}{4}&=15\end{align*}$$
Since $\frac{3}{4}<1$, the product is smaller than the original number.

$$\begin{align*}40\times\frac{8}{8}&=40\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Explain why the rule “multiply by the numerator and keep the denominator the same” works when multiplying a whole number and a fraction.

answer.short: Multiplication by a whole number is repeated addition. Adding equal fractions adds their numerators while keeping the denominator the same.
answer.worked:
Multiplication by a whole number is repeated addition of the same fraction, so the denominator stays the same and the numerator is multiplied by the whole number. Writing the whole number over 1 also gives
$$\begin{align*}n\times\frac{a}{b}&=\frac{n}{1}\times\frac{a}{b}\\&=\frac{n\times a}{1\times b}\\&=\frac{na}{b}.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The denominators must multiply to $12$, so the missing denominator is $12\div3=4$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{5}{4}&=\frac{2\times5}{3\times4}\\&=\frac{10}{12}\end{align*}$$

The missing numerator is $1$ because $2\times1=2$. The missing denominator is $2$ because $3\times2=6$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{2}&=\frac{2\times1}{3\times2}\\&=\frac{2}{6}\end{align*}$$

The denominators must multiply to $9$. One choice is $3$ and $3$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{5}{3}&=\frac{2\times5}{3\times3}\\&=\frac{10}{9}\end{align*}$$
The positive integer pairs $(1,9)$ and $(9,1)$ also work.

answer.short: Any pair with the first number double the second; for example, $2,\ 1$.
answer.worked:
Multiplying by $\frac12$ halves the first numerator. The first number must be double the second.
$$\begin{align*}\frac23\times\frac12&=\frac{2\times1}{3\times2}\\&=\frac26\\&=\frac13\end{align*}$$
For example, the boxes can contain $2$ and $1$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac7{10}\times\frac57&=\frac{7\times5}{10\times7}\\&=\frac{35}{70}\\&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
The missing fraction is $\frac57$; equivalent fractions also work.

answer.short: Any factor pair of $144$; for example, $12,\ 12$.
answer.worked:
The numerator of the product is $9\times2=18$. Since $\frac{18}{144}=\frac18$, the two denominators must multiply to $144$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac9{12}\times\frac2{12}&=\frac{9\times2}{12\times12}\\&=\frac{18}{144}\\&=\frac18\end{align*}$$
Any factor pair of $144$ works.

inlines.text: Jamie is catering for a large group and needs to quadruple the recipe.
How much flour and how much cream will she need?

answer.short: 7 cups of flour and 3 cups of cream
answer.worked:
Flour:
$$\begin{align*}1\frac{3}{4}\times4&=\frac{7}{4}\times\frac{4}{1}\\&=\frac{28}{4}\\&=7\end{align*}$$
Cream:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{3}{4}\times4&=\frac{3}{4}\times\frac{4}{1}\\&=\frac{12}{4}\\&=3\end{align*}$$
Jamie needs 7 cups of flour and 3 cups of cream.

content.prompt:
Granny spends one third of her weekly pension on Thursday night,
and one quarter of what remains on Friday.
What fraction of the original amount is left for her big night out on Saturday?

answer.worked:
After Thursday, $\frac{2}{3}$ remains. On Friday, she keeps $\frac{3}{4}$ of that amount.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Fraction remaining}&=\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{3}{4}\\&=\frac{1}{1}\times\frac{1}{2}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{align*}$$
She has half remaining.

answer.short: $112\frac{1}{2}$ glassfuls: 112 full glasses and half another glass.
answer.worked:

inlines.text: Using the clues provided, work out which two fractions are being discussed.
Altogether we consist of four different digits.
When added together our answer will still be a proper fraction.
When multiplied together you could carry out some cancelling.
The result of our product, when simplified, contains no new digits from our original four.
Three of our digits are prime numbers and the fourth digit is a cube number.

answer.short: Accept any one of these pairs: $\frac{2}{7}$ and $\frac{3}{8}$; $\frac{3}{7}$ and $\frac{2}{8}$; $\frac{2}{7}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$; $\frac{5}{7}$ and $\frac{2}{8}$. The clues do not identify a unique pair.
answer.worked:
The prime digits are chosen from $2,3,5,7$. The cube digit must be $8$: using $1$ would leave no common factor to cancel. Cancelling requires the prime digit $2$ together with $8$.

The following pairs satisfy every clue. Each fraction is proper, and cancelling $2$ with $8$ gives the simplified product.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{2}{7}+\frac{3}{8}&=\frac{37}{56}<1\\\frac{2}{7}\times\frac{3}{8}&=\frac{1}{7}\times\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{28}\\\frac{3}{7}+\frac{2}{8}&=\frac{19}{28}<1\\\frac{3}{7}\times\frac{2}{8}&=\frac{3}{7}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{28}\\\frac{2}{7}+\frac{5}{8}&=\frac{51}{56}<1\\\frac{2}{7}\times\frac{5}{8}&=\frac{1}{7}\times\frac{5}{4}=\frac{5}{28}\\\frac{5}{7}+\frac{2}{8}&=\frac{27}{28}<1\\\frac{5}{7}\times\frac{2}{8}&=\frac{5}{7}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{28}\end{align*}$$

The digit sets are $2,3,7,8$ or $2,5,7,8$. Each has three prime digits and the cube digit $8$, and neither simplified product introduces a new digit. The clues allow more than one pair.

content.prompt:
In a cricket test match, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the runs were scored in the first day, $\frac{1}{5}$ in the second day, $\frac{2}{5}$ in the third day, $\frac{7}{32}$ in the fourth day and remaining 21 runs on the last day.

How many runs were scored on each day?

answer.short: Day 1: 240 runs; Day 2: 288 runs; Day 3: 576 runs; Day 4: 315 runs; Day 5: 21 runs.
answer.worked:
The fraction scored on day 5 is
$$\begin{align*}
f_5 &= 1-\left(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{32}\right)\\
&=1-\left(\frac{80}{480}+\frac{96}{480}+\frac{192}{480}+\frac{105}{480}\right)\\
&=1-\frac{473}{480}\\
&=\frac{7}{480}.
\end{align*}$$
Let $x$ be the total number of runs.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{7}{480}x &=21\\
x &=21\times\frac{480}{7}\\
&=1440.
\end{align*}$$
The daily totals are
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Day 1} &=\frac{1}{6}\times1440=240\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 2} &=\frac{1}{5}\times1440=288\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 3} &=\frac{2}{5}\times1440=576\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 4} &=\frac{7}{32}\times1440=315\text{ runs}\\
\text{Day 5} &=21\text{ runs}.
\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The complete diagonal gives the common sum:
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\frac12+1\frac56+1\frac16\\&=\frac{15}{6}+\frac{11}{6}+\frac{7}{6}\\&=5\frac12.\end{align*}$$
Use the other diagonal, then the rows and columns:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Top right}&=\frac{11}{2}-\frac{11}{6}-3=\frac23\\\text{Top middle}&=\frac{11}{2}-\frac52-\frac23=2\frac13\\\text{Middle left}&=\frac{11}{2}-\frac52-3=0\\\text{Middle right}&=\frac{11}{2}-0-\frac{11}{6}=3\frac23\\\text{Bottom middle}&=\frac{11}{2}-3-\frac76=1\frac13.\end{align*}$$

The complete diagonal gives the common sum:

Use the other diagonal, then the rows and columns:

answer.worked:
Let $J$ and $K$ be Joanne’s and Kevin’s original numbers of marbles. Joanne owned $\frac35$ of the total and Kevin owned $\frac25$, so $J=\frac32K$. Afterwards, $J+6=2K$.

Kevin had 12 marbles and Joanne had 18 marbles.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply repeated halving to a quantity over five nights and explain why a positive remainder persists.

inlines.text: Johan found a 4-litre tub of ice cream. He stopped when he had eaten half of it.
The next night he again stopped when he had eaten half of what was there.
This went on for five nights in a row.
How much ice cream was left at the end of each of the five nights?
Would he ever have finished all the ice cream?

answer.short: Nights 1–5: $2\text{ L}$, $1\text{ L}$, $\frac12\text{ L}$, $\frac14\text{ L}$, $\frac18\text{ L}$. No; each night leaves half of the positive amount remaining.
answer.worked:
Half of the remaining ice cream is left each night.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Night 1}&: 4\times\frac12=2\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 2}&: 2\times\frac12=1\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 3}&: 1\times\frac12=\frac12\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 4}&: \frac12\times\frac12=\frac14\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 5}&: \frac14\times\frac12=\frac18\text{ L}
\end{align*}$$
After night $n$, the amount left is $4\times\left(\frac12\right)^n\text{ L}$. No; repeated halving always leaves a positive amount, so the ice cream never runs out under this process.

How many passengers were on the train when it left Alston?

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the initial number of passengers. After the first station, there are $\frac{x}{2}+135$ passengers. The second departure is $\frac{x}{3}$, referring to the passengers who arrived at the first station.
$$\begin{align*}\left(\frac{x}{2}+135\right)-\frac{x}{3}+110&=350\\\frac{x}{6}+245&=350\\\frac{x}{6}&=105\\x&=630\end{align*}$$
The train left Alston with 630 passengers.

answer.worked:
Write the equivalent fraction as $\frac{3a}{4a}$.

Write the equivalent fraction as $\frac{3a}{4a}$, using positive numerator and denominator.

answer.worked:
Replace each division after the first term with multiplication by its reciprocal. The first two terms give $\frac13\times3=1$. Since $81=3^4$, four further factors of $3$ are needed, giving $2+4=6$ terms.

Let $n$ be the number of occurrences of $\frac13$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac13\times3^{n-1}&=81\\3^{n-2}&=3^4\\n-2&=4\\n&=6\end{align*}$$

[Pedagogy review · High priority · opening-review · pf-d469c8002b]
Finding: The opening topic does not rehearse fraction simplification before its worked example uses it.
Breakdown: The transition from 4/12 to 1/3 depends on identifying a common divisor and dividing numerator and denominator by it.
Checked: There is no opening review or earlier booklet teaching. p4-teaching requests simplification but does not rehearse the prerequisite.
Assumes: Simplification is established prior knowledge. No calculator is assumed.
Proposed repair (add-review): Before p3-information, ask: 'Simplify 4/12, 6/8 and 6/10. State the number dividing both numerator and denominator in each case.' Answers: 1/3, 3/4, 3/5; divisors 4, 2, 2.
Done when: Students rehearse common-divisor simplification before the worked example.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · unsupported-transition · pf-51b3d86fc1]
Finding: Whole-number subtraction begins before the booklet supplies the conversion into matching fractional units.
Breakdown: The preceding instruction models fraction operands only. Students need the connection from 1 to 3/3, and from 2 to 10/5, to apply that method.
Checked: p3-guided-c and p5-q3-f establish fractions equalling one whole but do not model rewriting the whole-number operand. p8-q9 supplies a relevant model after these tasks.
Assumes: Equivalent fractions are prior knowledge; the new operand form needs a connecting cue. No calculator is assumed.
Also affects: p7-q6-o
Proposed repair (add-cue): Before p7-q6-g, write: 'Express the whole number in matching fractional units first: 1 = 3/3, so 1 − 1/3 = 3/3 − 1/3.' Before p7-q6-o, add: 'Two wholes contain ten fifths: 2 = 10/5.'
Done when: Both whole-number operand forms have a conversion cue before use.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · duplicate-question · pf-6f65d1afa7]
Finding: The same missing-number task appears twice without an instructional purpose.
Breakdown: Both parts ask students to complete 1 = □ + 3/5 with identical response forms.
Checked: Compared the complete prompts and parent instruction. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated.
Assumes: The unchanged repetition is accidental.
Also affects: p9-q15-d
Proposed repair (remove-question): Remove p9-q15-d.
Done when: Only one copy remains.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · opening-review · pf-20324477f3]
Finding: Equivalent-fraction scaling is not rehearsed before the related-denominator examples use it.
Breakdown: Following the examples requires converting 1/4 into 2/8 and 3/12 by scaling both entries together.
Checked: The preceding topic practises same-denominator operations and reduction, rather than generating equivalents by multiplication. p11-example-response states the scaling rule after the introductory examples.
Assumes: Equivalent-fraction scaling is prior knowledge. No calculator is assumed.
Also affects: p10-example-right
Proposed repair (add-review): Before p10-information, ask: 'Complete 1/3 = □/6, 2/5 = □/15 and 3/4 = □/12. State the multiplier applied to both entries.' Numerators: 2, 6, 9; multipliers: 2, 3, 3.
Done when: Students independently rehearse equal scaling before the examples.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · duplicate-question · pf-a04c5b6803]
Finding: The unscaffolded calculation 1/4 + 1/3 appears twice without an explicit instructional purpose.
Breakdown: The operands, operation and required response are unchanged.
Checked: Compared both complete tasks and parent instructions. p22-q6-e belongs to a useful consecutive variation sequence, but there is no explicit purpose for repeating its earlier copy.
Assumes: The duplicate exception applies; the variation sequence should be preserved.
Also affects: p22-q6-e
Proposed repair (remove-question): Remove p20-q3-g and retain p22-q6-e within its variation sequence.
Done when: The unchanged task appears once and the p22 variation sequence remains intact.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · example-choice · pf-dce262ef2f]
Finding: Separate-parts subtraction does not model the exchange that produces the final mixed-number answer.
Breakdown: The first demonstration jumps from 3 − 1/12 to 2 11/12 without showing the source of the reduced whole part and the eleven twelfths.
Checked: Earlier whole-minus-fraction practice establishes calculations, but no preceding teaching demonstrates this exchange as the completion step of separate-parts subtraction. p28 repeats the omitted step.
Assumes: Students are learning the alternate method from these demonstrations. Calculator use does not supply the explanation.
Also affects: p28-q4-worked-part
Proposed repair (add-cue): After 3 − 1/12, insert: 'Exchange one whole for twelve twelfths: 3 − 1/12 = 2 + 12/12 − 1/12 = 2 11/12.'
Done when: The first demonstration explicitly accounts for both parts of the final answer.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · difficulty-jump · pf-f8f99c8503]
Finding: The missing-number exercise starts with two unknown denominators before its more constrained tasks.
Breakdown: Students move from forward calculations and earlier single missing values to choosing two unit-fraction denominators and testing their difference. The existing fixed-denominator tasks provide intermediate demands.
Checked: Earlier missing-number questions do not model this two-denominator search. p31-q10-c fixes equal denominators; p31-q10-b fixes unequal denominators. These can precede p31-q10-a without changing any task.
Assumes: Students have not already developed a two-denominator search routine. Calculator availability does not determine the repair.
Also affects: p31-q10-b, p31-q10-c, p31-q10-d
Proposed repair (reorder): Present p31-q10 in the order c, b, a, d.
Done when: Fixed-denominator missing-numerator tasks precede the two-denominator search.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · missing-prerequisite · pf-1eb8c74341]
Finding: Addition-and-subtraction mixed practice requires fraction multiplication and division before their teaching.
Breakdown: These parts require constructing a product, solving a fraction division, and finding a missing mixed-number factor. The preceding addition and subtraction methods do not supply those operations.
Checked: All preceding teaching was searched. Multiplication methods begin at p43 and p49; mixed-number multiplication follows at p54, and reciprocal division at p67. p36-q10 has separable equations, so moving these parts does not break a shared calculation.
Assumes: Fraction multiplication and division are intended learning in this booklet rather than assumed completed instruction.
Also affects: p36-q10-d, p36-q10-h

3. Add or subtract the numerators.
4. Simplify if possible.

entries.description: Multiplying and Dividing by Rational Numbers

Multiplying by Rational Numbers
When you multiply a number by:
• A number less than 1, your answer is smaller than your starting number.
• The number 1, your answer equals your starting number.
• A number greater than 1, your answer is larger than your starting number.

entries.description:
Using the clues provided, work out which two fractions are being discussed.
• We are two proper fractions.
• Altogether we consist of four different digits.
• When added together our answer will still be a proper fraction.
• When multiplied together you could carry out some cancelling.
• The result of our product, when simplified, contains no new digits from our original four.

expectedAnswer.worked: Let \(\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}\). \(\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{x}=\frac{x-6}{6x}\). \(y=\frac{6x}{x-6}=6+\frac{36}{x-6}\). For \(y\) to be an integer, \((x-6)\) must be a factor of 36. Factors of 36 yielding unique pairs: \(x-6=2,3,4,6\). Sub \(x=8,9,10,12\) to find pairs: \(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{24},\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{18},\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{15},\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}\).
